Sampled HR@10 measures ranking against the specified negatives; it can reverse model comparisons relative to full-catalog evaluation. Keep the pinned 99-negative candidate sets unchanged and interpret gains within that protocol. Probability calibration alone does not establish ranking improvement: any strictly increasing score transformation preserves HR@10, apart from numerical ties. [Krichene and Rendle](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/)

Negative-sampled BCE can produce overconfident probabilities; gBCE changes training to mitigate this and may improve learned rankings. Evidence includes BERT4Rec trained with sampled negatives, but does not guarantee gains on these Amazon categories. Proposed priority: a small controlled BCE-versus-gBCE × negative-count ablation, preserving the corrected BERT4Rec backbone, masked-target task, seeds, training schedule and checkpoint-selection rule. Record GPU cost and actual negatives processed, since increasing negative count changes compute. Retain one trained checkpoint per category. [Petrov and Macdonald](https://theses.gla.ac.uk/85270/2/2025petrovphd.pdf)

For uncertainty diagnostics, retain paired per-user hit indicators. Bootstrap users within each category, using identical resampled indices for both models, then average the four category differences equally; report the macro-HR@10 difference and percentile interval. This estimates user-sampling uncertainty conditional on fixed candidates and fitted models, not training-seed or candidate-sampling variability. Repeated checkpoint/trial selection on the same validation users creates optimism; an ordinary bootstrap of the selected winner does not remove it. Predeclare a limited comparison/checkpoint schedule, disclose selection counts, and treat intervals as descriptive after selection; leave independent final evaluation to the host. [Cawley and Talbot](https://www.jmlr.org/beta/papers/v11/cawley10a.html)
